lesson.title: 1. Music and Nostalgia
lesson.context: ***Context:*** *Chloe is helping her friend Sam clear out his old bedroom at his parents’ house. Sam finds a box under the bed.*
lines: Sam
Oh, look what I’ve found. My old MP3 player. It’s been **gathering dust** under here for years.
Chloe
**That brings back memories.** Does it still work?
Sam
Let me charge it… Yeah, it does. Everything on here is from about 2010.
Chloe
Go on, **hit play**. **For old times’ sake.**
Sam
OK, this one. I **had it on repeat** for the whole of Year 11. I still **know every word by heart**.
Chloe
I remember this! It was **all over the radio** that year. It’s so **catchy**. It used to **get stuck in my head** for days.
Sam
It’s pretty **cheesy**, though.
Chloe
Very. But I’ve always **had a soft spot for** it. We used to **sing it at the top of our lungs** on the school bus.
Sam
It’s funny. I haven’t heard it in years, but it **takes me straight back**. I can **vividly remember** the smell of the school canteen.
Chloe
Music’s good at that. It’s like **a trip down memory lane**.
Sam
To be honest, I think I miss that time more than the song. Life was so much simpler. No rent, no deadlines.
Chloe
Ah, **the good old days**.
Sam
Although, **in hindsight**, I complained about exams all the time.
Chloe
We all did. I read somewhere that the songs we hear as teenagers **stay with us for life**. That’s why your dad still plays the same three bands from the eighties.
Sam
And tells me **they don’t make music like they used to**.
Chloe
Every generation says that.
Sam
I know. I’ve started saying it too. It **makes me feel old**.
Chloe
I think we **look back through rose-tinted glasses**.
Sam
**Fair enough.** Some of these have **stood the test of time**, though. Others… **haven’t aged well** at all.
Chloe
So, are you going to throw it away?
Sam
No, I’ll **hang on to** it. Everyone needs **a bit of nostalgia** sometimes.

lesson.title: 2. Fans and indie music
lesson.context: ***Context:*** *Mia and Jack are colleagues. It’s Monday morning, and Mia looks very tired.*
lines: Jack
You seem a bit tired today. Busy weekend?
Mia
Not really. I **stayed up** late last night trying to get concert tickets. The website **kept crashing**, but I got two **in the end**. They’re right at the back, but I’m just happy to be going.
Jack
Is this for that boy band you really like?
Mia
Yes, **that’s the one**. I know it sounds a bit silly.
Jack
It’s not silly, but **I don’t really get it**. Is it really **worth losing sleep over**?
Mia

For me, it is. It’s not just about the music. A few years ago, I was **going through a rough patch** at work, and their songs really **got me through it**. I’ve also made some close friends through the **fan community**.
Jack
So it’s more about the people than the band.
Mia
Kind of. It gives me **a sense of belonging**. When the whole stadium is singing along, you **feel like part of something bigger**. It’s **hard to put into words**.
Jack
That sounds nice, actually. I’m just **not a big fan of** crowds. I prefer small **gigs**.
Mia
Right, you’re more **into** indie music, aren’t you?
Jack

Yeah. I like finding bands **before they make it big**. And small gigs feel really **raw**. There are only about thirty people in the room, and you can hear every word. It’s easy to **lose yourself in the music**.
Mia
**I can see the appeal.**
Jack
The lyrics also **hit close to home**. They’re less about love and more about **everyday struggles**, like paying rent or not knowing what to do with your life.
Mia
That sounds a bit sad.
Jack
Sometimes it is. But it’s **comforting** to know someone else feels the same way.
Mia
**Funnily enough**, that’s exactly how I feel about my band. We just like different sounds.
Jack
Maybe we’re **not so different after all**.

head: Purposes
Phrases
rows:

***It’s hard to put into words, but it makes me feel…***

homework.title: Part 3: Listening
homework.intro: Listen to a short radio segment about music and memory, then do Parts A and B.
homework.podcast: 🎧 Why old songs stay with us

script.text: Have you ever noticed that the songs you loved as a teenager still feel special, even if you'd never choose to listen to them today? You're not alone. Researchers call this the "reminiscence bump". ==Most people remember more events from their teens and early twenties than from any other time in their lives==, and the music from those years tends to stay with us the longest.

Part of the reason is that ==so many things happen for the first time in those years==: first friendships, first heartbreak, first time living away from home. ==Our emotions are stronger, and the songs we hear become linked to those feelings==. So when an old song comes on, it's not just the melody we're reacting to. It's the memory of who we were.

My own example is a little embarrassing. When I was fifteen, ==I was obsessed with a boy band==. I had posters all over my bedroom wall, and I queued for six hours to see them live. If you'd told me then that ==I'd be a jazz lover at thirty==, I'd have laughed. ==These days, I almost never listen to that band==. But last month, one of their songs came on in a café, and ==I suddenly felt fifteen again==. I could almost smell my old school bag.

Interestingly, experts say ==this effect isn't really about whether the music is good==. Some of the songs we remember most fondly are, honestly, pretty average. ==What matters is when we heard them==. That's also why our parents often insist that ==music was better in their day==. They're not completely wrong. They're just remembering the songs together with the best years of their lives.
So next time someone laughs at your old playlist, don't apologise. It's not really a playlist. ==It's a diary.==

options: The habit of only listening to music from your teenage years.
The tendency to remember more from your teens and early twenties than from other periods.
The embarrassing feeling you get when you hear an old song.
questions.why: “Most people remember more events from their teens and early twenties than from any other time in their lives.”

questions.q: Why do songs from these years become so memorable?
options: The songs become connected to strong feelings from new experiences.
Teenagers listen to music much more often than adults do.
Songs from that period usually have simpler, catchier melodies.
questions.why: “Our emotions are stronger, and the songs we hear become linked to those feelings.”

questions.q: What do we learn about the speaker?
options: She still listens to the boy band she loved as a teenager.
She went to a café specifically to listen to her old favourite songs.
Her taste in music has changed a lot since she was fifteen.
questions.why: “I'd be a jazz lover at thirty… These days, I almost never listen to that band.”

questions.q: What happened when she heard the song in the café?
options: She felt embarrassed and wanted to leave.
Her teenage years came back to her very clearly.
She realised the song was better than she remembered.
questions.why: “I suddenly felt fifteen again. I could almost smell my old school bag.”

questions.q: According to experts, which songs do we remember most fondly?
options: The ones that are of the highest quality.
The ones our parents played when we were children.
The ones we heard at a particular stage of our lives.
questions.why: “What matters is when we heard them.”

questions.q: What does the speaker mean when she says an old playlist is “a diary”?
options: It records important moments and feelings from our past.
People should write down the songs they listen to every day.
It shows how much our taste in music has improved.
questions.why: “It's not really a playlist. It's a diary.”
